title: Eggs Benedict
subtitle: Poached eggs and ham on English muffins with hollandaise
excerpt: Eggs Benedict sits poached eggs and grilled ham on toasted English muffins, finished with warm hollandaise sauce. The dish has three distinct components, each with its own timing. Done well, it is one of the best things on a brunch table.
sourceNotes: American brunch tradition. The dish is associated with Delmonico's restaurant in New York and stockbroker Lemuel Benedict, who is said to have requested the combination as a hangover cure in the 1890s. Hollandaise is documented in French culinary tradition from the nineteenth century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Hollandaise can be made up to 30 minutes ahead and kept warm over a pan of warm water off the heat. Do not reheat it. Poach the eggs just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: A warm emulsified sauce made from egg yolks, lemon juice, and clarified or melted butter. The yolks are whisked over gentle heat until thick, then the butter is added gradually to form a smooth, glossy sauce.

Cooking in simmering liquid (not boiling) so the food cooks gently without breaking apart. Eggs are poached in barely simmering water with a little vinegar to help the white set around the yolk quickly.

content.text: Eggs Benedict is three things built in the right order: the
the eggs is the step that catches people out. Fresh eggs with compact whites poach cleanly. Older eggs spread into rags. Use the freshest eggs you can find.

items.prepNote: grilled until just cooked, or use good ham
clarified or melted and cooled slightly

content.text: You will need 4 English muffins (available in most supermarkets). A double boiler or a heatproof bowl set over a saucepan works for the hollandaise; the bowl should not touch the water.

Bring a small pan of water to a gentle simmer. Set a heatproof bowl on top, not touching the water. Add the 3 egg yolks and {{lemon-juice}} of lemon juice to the bowl. Whisk constantly for 3 to 4 minutes until the mixture is pale and has doubled in volume, and leaves a thick ribbon when the whisk is lifted.

Remove the bowl from the heat. Whisk in {{unsalted-butter}} of melted butter, starting with a few drops at a time, then adding it in a slow, steady stream. The sauce will thicken as you add the butter. Season with salt and white pepper. Taste and adjust the lemon. Keep the bowl in a warm spot.

Fill a wide saucepan with about 8 cm of water. Add the {{cider-vinegar}} of cider vinegar. Bring to a very gentle simmer: small bubbles on the base, not a rolling boil. Split and toast the muffins. Grill or pan-fry the bacon.

Crack the 4 eggs one at a time into a cup. Create a gentle swirl in the water with a spoon and slide one egg into the centre. Poach for 3 minutes for a set white and runny yolk. Lift out with a slotted spoon onto kitchen paper.
Lay a slice of bacon on each muffin half. Set a poached egg on top. Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of hollandaise over each egg. Serve at once.

items.symptom: Hollandaise splitting (oil separating from the eggs)
items.cause: Heat too high or butter added too quickly.
items.fix: If the sauce splits, remove from heat, start with one fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl, and gradually whisk the broken sauce into it. The new yolk re-emulsifies the mixture.

items.symptom: Poached eggs spreading in the water
items.cause: Eggs not fresh enough, or water boiling too vigorously.
items.fix: Use the freshest eggs possible. Keep the water at a bare simmer. Swirling the water before adding the egg helps the white wrap around the yolk.

items.symptom: Timing chaos — everything ready at different times
items.fix: Make the hollandaise first and keep it warm. Poach the eggs last, immediately before serving, with everything else already plated.

items.symptom: Yolk set solid rather than runny
items.cause: Overcooked. Poaching water too hot or eggs left in too long.
items.fix: Three minutes in barely simmering water gives a set white and soft yolk. Check the water is not boiling.

content.text: Eggs Florentine replaces the bacon with wilted spinach, making it vegetarian. Eggs Royale uses smoked salmon. A Muffin Benedict uses sautéed mushrooms and tomato. The hollandaise can have a teaspoon of Dijon whisked in at the end for a sharper note.

Eggs Benedict is the canonical American brunch dish, associated with Manhattan hotel dining rooms and weekend indulgence. It requires attention and coordination, which is part of the appeal as a weekend project. The combination of soft poached egg, salty meat, and rich butter sauce has been working since the 1890s for good reason.
